category.name: Construction Equipment
category.tagline: LiuGong earthmoving, roadbuilding and quarry machines, supported where they work
category.intro: Excavators, wheel loaders, bulldozers, motor graders, backhoe loaders, rollers and mining trucks for Nigerian road, building, quarry, port and farm projects. Chanrai Nigeria supplies LiuGong equipment from its base in Isolo, Lagos, and sends its technicians to the machine, so most service work is done on the customer's own site.
category.salesBlurb: Sales helps you match a machine to the job. We look at material, haul distances, the ground and your daily output, then quote a LiuGong model and configuration that fits, along with the attachments and support plan it needs.
category.serviceBlurb: Field technicians travel to your site with diagnostic tools and service kits. They carry out scheduled maintenance, fault-finding and repairs where the machine is working, so you are not paying to move it to a workshop.
category.partsBlurb: We stock genuine LiuGong OEM parts: filters, wear parts, undercarriage, ground-engaging tools and major components.

brand.name: LiuGong
brand.about: LiuGong is a Chinese maker of construction machinery. It was founded in 1958 in Liuzhou, in Guangxi, where it still has its headquarters, and it is listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange. The company is best known for wheel loaders and now builds a full range: excavators, dozers, graders, rollers, skid steers, backhoe loaders and mining trucks, among others. In Africa it supports dealers through a Middle East and Africa regional organisation that also handles parts and training.
highlights: Founded in 1958 in Liuzhou, China; listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange (000528)
One of the world's leading wheel loader manufacturers
Offers 19 product lines across earthmoving, roadbuilding, lifting and material handling
Owns Dressta (Poland), a dozer maker, and runs driveline and engine joint ventures with ZF and Cummins
Its wheel loaders and excavators rank among the best-selling machines of their kind in sub-Saharan Africa
The Middle East and Africa range covers wheel loaders, excavators, rollers, motor graders, bulldozers, skid steer loaders, backhoe loaders, mining trucks and cranes

families.name: Excavators
families.summary: Tracked hydraulic excavators from 22 to 77 tonnes for digging, trenching, loading trucks, quarry and mining work.
families.howItWorks:
A crawler excavator has two main parts: a **lower undercarriage** of steel tracks driven by hydraulic travel motors, and an **upper structure** that turns a full 360° on a large slewing bearing. The upper structure carries the cab, the engine, the hydraulic pumps and the digging equipment.

The diesel engine does not drive the tracks or the bucket directly. It turns **variable-displacement hydraulic pumps**, which turn engine power into a flow of oil under pressure. A **main control valve** sends that oil to whichever function the operator selects: boom, arm (stick) and bucket cylinders, the swing motor or the travel motors. The joysticks are low-pressure **pilot controls**. They move spools in the main valve, so the operator can meter flow smoothly and run several functions together, such as swinging while raising the boom.

Digging force comes from hydraulic pressure acting on cylinder area. The bucket cylinder curls the bucket into the material, and the arm cylinder pulls it towards the machine. Spec sheets quote both as separate ISO **bucket** and **arm digging forces**. Many machines have a short-term **power boost**, which raises relief pressure for hard digging. **Working modes** match engine speed and pump output to the task. A power mode suits heavy production, an economy mode suits general digging, and a fine mode gives slow, precise moves for lifting or trimming.

The **counterweight** at the rear balances the load in the bucket. **Track width and length** spread the machine's weight, so an excavator can work on soft or uneven ground where a wheeled machine would sink.

keyComponents.name: Boom
keyComponents.role: The main lifting arm, pinned to the upper structure and raised and lowered by one or two hydraulic cylinders.

keyComponents.name: Arm (stick)
keyComponents.role: Links the boom to the bucket and sets digging depth and reach; its cylinder supplies the arm digging force.

keyComponents.name: Bucket and ground-engaging tools
keyComponents.role: Does the cutting and carrying; its teeth and adapters are wear parts that need replacing regularly.

keyComponents.name: Main hydraulic pumps
keyComponents.role: Engine-driven pumps that supply pressurised oil to every function on the machine.

keyComponents.name: Main control valve
keyComponents.role: Sends oil to cylinders and motors according to the operator's pilot joystick inputs.

keyComponents.name: Swing bearing and swing motor
keyComponents.role: Let the upper structure rotate 360° and hold it steady during digging.

keyComponents.name: Undercarriage
keyComponents.role: Tracks, rollers, idlers, sprockets and travel motors that carry and move the machine; it accounts for a large share of the machine's lifetime running costs.

keyComponents.name: Counterweight
keyComponents.role: Balances the load and the digging forces so the machine stays stable.

Ask about bucket options. A general-purpose bucket suits soil, while a heavy-duty or rock bucket is needed for blasted rock and laterite.
If you plan to run a hammer, shear or other attachment, confirm the machine has auxiliary hydraulic piping and the right flow settings.
Choose track shoe width for the ground. Wider shoes float better on swampy Niger Delta soils, while narrower shoes last longer on rock.
Factor in transport: the shipping width and weight decide what low-bed trailer and permits you need.

faq.q: What size excavator do I need?
faq.a: It depends on the material, how deep you need to dig, and what the machine will load. Machines of 20–25 t are the general-purpose workhorses for roads and building sites. A 35 t machine suits heavier digging and truck loading. Machines of 50 t and above suit quarry faces, mass excavation and mining. Tell us about the job and we will recommend a size.

faq.q: What is the difference between bucket and arm digging force?
faq.a: Bucket digging force comes from the bucket cylinder curling the bucket into the material. Arm digging force comes from the arm cylinder pulling the bucket towards the machine. Both are measured to an ISO standard, so you can compare figures across brands.

faq.q: Can an excavator run a hydraulic hammer?
faq.a: Yes, as long as it has auxiliary hydraulic piping and the flow and pressure are set to suit the hammer. We can check compatibility and set the machine up during commissioning.

faq.q: How often should the undercarriage be inspected?
faq.a: Check track tension and look for visible damage every day. Carry out a detailed undercarriage inspection at regular intervals, often around every 250 hours. Tension that is too tight or too loose speeds up wear, especially in abrasive laterite and sand.

faq.q: Do you service excavators on site?
faq.a: Yes. Our model is built around field service. Technicians travel to the machine for scheduled maintenance, diagnosis and repairs, so it does not need to come to a workshop.

families.name: Wheel Loaders
families.summary: Articulated wheel loaders from 16 to 31 tonnes for loading, stockpiling and moving material around quarries, ports, plants and sites.
families.howItWorks:
A wheel loader is a four-wheel-drive machine with a hydraulic bucket at the front. Its job is to scoop loose material, carry it and dump it into a truck, hopper or stockpile.

Most loaders are **articulated**. The chassis is split into front and rear frames joined by a central hinge, and two steering cylinders fold the machine at that hinge, typically about 35–40° each way. The rear wheels follow the front wheels, so the loader turns tightly for its size and the bucket always faces where the machine is heading.

Power travels from the diesel engine through a **torque converter**, a fluid coupling that multiplies torque when the wheels meet resistance. When the bucket is driven into a pile, the converter lets the engine keep its speed while the wheels slow down and push harder. This is why loaders dig so well without stalling. A **powershift transmission** then changes gears under load, with no clutch pedal. Drive goes to **heavy-duty axles** front and rear, and some machines add limited-slip or locking differentials for traction in mud.

The loading equipment is a **lift arm** (boom) with lift cylinders and a **tilt linkage** that curls and dumps the bucket. A common design is the Z-bar linkage, which gives strong breakout force. An engine-driven pump powers both these functions and the steering. On spec sheets, **breakout force** tells you how hard the bucket can tear into a pile. **Tipping load** is the weight at which the machine would tip forward, and safe working loads are set well below it. **Dump clearance** tells you which truck heights you can load over.

keyComponents.name: Articulation joint
keyComponents.role: The centre hinge between the front and rear frames, which lets the loader steer by folding in the middle.

keyComponents.name: Torque converter
keyComponents.role: A fluid coupling between the engine and the transmission that multiplies torque when the bucket pushes into a pile.

keyComponents.name: Powershift transmission
keyComponents.role: Changes gear and direction under load without a foot clutch.

keyComponents.name: Axles and differentials
keyComponents.role: Carry the machine's weight and send drive to all four wheels.

keyComponents.name: Lift arm and tilt linkage
keyComponents.role: Raise, curl and dump the bucket; the geometry sets breakout force and dump reach.

keyComponents.name: Bucket and cutting edge
keyComponents.role: Chosen to suit the material; the bolt-on edges and teeth are wear parts.

keyComponents.name: Hydraulic pump and control valve
keyComponents.role: Supply oil to the lift, tilt and steering circuits.

keyComponents.name: Tyres
keyComponents.role: A major operating cost; the tread pattern and ply rating should match the ground conditions.

Handling bulk cargo (clinker, fertiliser, grains) at Apapa, Tin Can and Onne ports

choosingTips: Match the bucket size to the material density. Light materials such as sand and grain take a bigger bucket than heavy blasted rock.
Check that dump clearance is enough to load over the side boards of your tipper trucks.
Size the loader to the truck. Three to four passes per truck usually keeps both machines working efficiently.
For quarry and rock work, specify rock buckets, protective guards and rock-pattern tyres.
Short-cycle yard loading favours a smaller, nimbler loader. Load-and-carry over longer distances favours a larger machine with higher travel speed.
Ask about attachment options: quick couplers, pallet forks, log grapples and high-tip buckets.

Use the reversing alarm and camera where fitted. Reversing is the main cause of loader accidents on yards

faq.q: What does the model number of a LiuGong wheel loader tell me?
faq.a: Higher numbers mean larger machines in the range. For example, the 890T is a 31-tonne-class loader. The ZL50CN follows an older naming: the 50 stands for its 5-tonne rated load. Always compare the actual operating weight, bucket size and tipping load rather than relying on the model number alone.

faq.q: What is the difference between tipping load and rated load?
faq.a: Tipping load is the weight in the bucket at which the machine would start to tip forward. The safe rated operating load is set well below that figure to leave a stability margin, so never plan work around the tipping load.

faq.q: Which bucket should I use for sand versus rock?
faq.a: Use a larger general-purpose or light-material bucket for sand and other loose, light materials. For blasted rock, use a smaller, reinforced rock bucket with teeth and a protected edge, which limits stress and wear on the machine.

faq.q: How can I reduce tyre costs?
faq.a: Keep the correct inflation pressure, clear rock spillage from loading areas, avoid wheel spin when entering the pile, and choose a tread pattern that suits the ground. Tyres are often one of the biggest running costs on a loader.

faq.q: Can you service a loader at our quarry or port?
faq.a: Yes. Scheduled services and most repairs are done on site by our field technicians, so the machine stays close to where it works.

families.name: Bulldozers
families.summary: Crawler dozers for pushing, spreading and ripping, used for land clearing, road formation and quarry overburden.
families.howItWorks:
A bulldozer (crawler tractor) is built to push. It has a heavy steel frame on long tracks, a wide **blade** at the front and, in most cases, a **ripper** at the rear. Its tracks spread a large weight over a big ground area, so it gets the grip it needs to shove soil, rock and vegetation.

The diesel engine drives through a **torque converter** and a **powershift transmission**, much as a wheel loader does. When the blade meets heavy resistance, the converter multiplies torque so the engine keeps running instead of stalling. From the transmission, power goes to **steering clutches and brakes**, or to a differential steering unit on some designs, and then through **final drives** to the sprockets that turn each track. To turn, the machine slows or stops one track and keeps driving the other.

The blade is raised, lowered and tilted by hydraulic cylinders. Blade shape decides the job. A **straight blade** cuts and grades well. A **semi-U blade** has curved wings that hold more material for pushing. A **full-U blade** carries the largest load over longer distances in loose material. **Blade capacity** (m³) on the spec sheet tells you roughly how much one pass can move.

The **ripper** is one or more hardened shanks that the operator drives into the ground to break up compacted laterite, soft rock or old pavement so the blade can move it. A single-shank ripper reaches deeper, and a multi-shank ripper breaks a wider strip. **Ground pressure** (kPa) shows how well the dozer will float on soft ground. Lower is better in swamp and wet clay.

keyComponents.name: Blade
keyComponents.role: Cuts, pushes and spreads material; its shape (straight, semi-U or full-U) sets capacity and grading ability.

keyComponents.name: Ripper
keyComponents.role: Rear shank or shanks that break up hard ground, soft rock and old pavement ahead of dozing.

keyComponents.name: Torque converter and powershift transmission
keyComponents.role: Multiply torque under heavy load and give clutchless gear and direction changes.

keyComponents.name: Steering clutches and brakes
keyComponents.role: Slow or stop one track so the dozer turns.

keyComponents.name: Final drives and sprockets
keyComponents.role: Reduce speed and multiply torque at each track.

keyComponents.name: Undercarriage
keyComponents.role: Track chains, shoes, rollers and idlers; the largest wear-cost item on a dozer.

keyComponents.name: Blade lift and tilt cylinders
keyComponents.role: Raise, lower and tilt the blade for cutting, spreading and side-slope work.

Add a ripper if you will meet hard laterite, weathered rock or old asphalt. A single shank penetrates deepest.
On swampy or wet clay sites, look for lower ground pressure or wider track shoes.
Larger dozers move material faster but cost more to transport. Check low-bed availability and road permits.
Remember that undercarriage wear in abrasive sand and laterite drives running costs, so plan undercarriage inspections from day one.

maintenance.note: These intervals reflect general industry practice and are a guide only. Always follow the LiuGong operation and maintenance manual for your model and serial number. Heavy ripping and abrasive soils call for shorter intervals.

safety: Walk the area before clearing to find hidden ditches, soft spots, stumps and buried services
Watch for falling trees and branches during land clearing, and make sure the cab protective structure (ROPS/FOPS) is in place
Do not work along the edge of a fill or bank without a safe margin
On steep slopes, travel straight up or down rather than across
Lower the blade and ripper to the ground before leaving the machine
Keep everyone clear of the rear when ripping or reversing

faq.q: What is the difference between a straight blade and a U-blade?
faq.a: A straight blade cuts, levels and grades well. A U-blade has curved side wings that keep material from spilling off the ends, so it carries more per pass over longer pushes but is less suited to fine grading.

faq.q: Do I need a ripper?
faq.a: Fit one if your sites have hard laterite, weathered rock, old pavement or compacted fill. Ripping first lets the blade move material faster and lowers stress on the machine.

faq.q: Why does a dozer need so much undercarriage maintenance?
faq.a: The tracks carry the whole machine and grind against abrasive soil all day. Correct track tension, regular cleaning and measuring wear help the undercarriage reach its full life, and that is where much of a dozer's running cost is decided.

faq.q: Can a dozer work in swampy ground?
faq.a: Yes, within limits. Lower ground pressure and wider track shoes help a dozer float on soft soil. Tell us about your site conditions and we will advise on the right configuration.

families.name: Motor Graders
families.summary: Motor graders that shape, level and finish road formations, shoulders, drains and site platforms to accurate grade.
families.howItWorks:
A motor grader is a precision levelling machine. A long front frame carries a **moldboard** (blade) mounted under the middle of the machine on a rotating **circle**. The cab, the engine and a set of **tandem drive wheels** sit at the rear.

The operator can position the blade in almost any direction. **Lift cylinders** on each side raise or lower each end on its own, which sets the crossfall or camber. The **circle** turns the blade to an angle, so the material it cuts rolls off to one side and forms a windrow. **Side-shift** slides the blade out past the wheels to cut ditches and shoulders. The blade can also be tilted to change how it cuts. Together these controls let a skilled operator cut, spread and fine-trim to tolerances of a few centimetres.

The engine drives the rear tandem wheels through a **torque converter** and a **powershift transmission**, which has several forward gears for slow, high-force cutting and faster gears for travel between sites. The tandems are mounted in **oscillating boxes**, so all four rear wheels stay on the ground over uneven surfaces. A long wheelbase helps too, because the machine averages out bumps instead of copying them into the surface.

Many graders are **articulated** between the front frame and the rear unit, and the front wheels can **lean**. Both help the machine turn tightly and hold a straight line against the side load the angled blade creates. Optional **rear rippers** or **front scarifiers** break up hard surfaces before shaping, and a **front dozer blade** can be fitted for spreading.

keyComponents.role: Cuts, moves and finishes material to the required grade and shape.

keyComponents.name: Circle and drawbar
keyComponents.role: Carry the blade and rotate it to angle material off to one side.

keyComponents.name: Blade lift and side-shift cylinders

keyComponents.name: Tandem drive
keyComponents.role: Oscillating rear wheel pairs that keep traction and stability on uneven ground.

keyComponents.name: Torque converter and powershift transmission
keyComponents.role: Give smooth power for cutting and a wide spread of gears for working and travel.

keyComponents.name: Articulation joint and front wheel lean
keyComponents.role: Allow tight turns and offset the side load from the angled blade.

keyComponents.name: Rear ripper or front scarifier (optional)
keyComponents.role: Loosen compacted or hard surfaces before shaping.

Lower the blade to the ground before leaving the cab

faq.q: Why can't a dozer do a grader's job?
faq.a: A dozer is built for force. A grader is built for accuracy: its long wheelbase and adjustable blade let it trim to a precise level and camber, which road specifications require.

faq.q: What does blade pull mean?
faq.a: Blade pull is the pulling force the grader can produce at the blade, and it shows how much cutting work the machine can handle. Heavier, more powerful graders produce more of it.

faq.q: Do I need a ripper on my grader?
faq.a: It helps if you regularly break up hard, compacted laterite or old road surfaces before reshaping them. For maintenance grading on loose surfaces it is often unnecessary.

faq.q: Can a grader be fitted with automatic grade control?
faq.a: Many graders can be fitted with GPS or laser grade-control systems. Ask us about compatibility for the model you are considering.

families.name: Backhoe Loaders
families.summary: Wheeled machines with a loader at the front and a digging backhoe at the rear: two machines in one for municipal, utility and small-contractor work.
families.howItWorks:
A backhoe loader combines a **front loader** and a **rear excavator arm** (the backhoe) on a tractor-style wheeled chassis. The operator's seat swivels to face whichever end is in use.

At the front, a **loader bucket** on two lift arms scoops, carries and loads material much as a small wheel loader does. At the rear, the **backhoe** has a boom, a dipper (stick) and a small bucket on a **swing frame** that pivots side to side. The backhoe digs trenches, foundations and pits, and lifts pipes into place. Before digging, the operator lowers two hydraulic **stabiliser legs** at the rear and rests the front bucket on the ground. This lifts weight off the tyres and gives a stable, three-point base for digging.

A single engine-driven **hydraulic pump** powers both ends through separate control valves. Unlike an excavator, the backhoe does not rotate a full 360°. Its swing is limited to an arc behind the machine. For travel, power goes from the engine through a **torque converter** and a **shuttle transmission**, which reverses direction quickly for loader work. Drive goes to the rear wheels, or to all four on 4WD versions. With road-legal speeds, a backhoe can drive between jobs without a low-bed, which is why it suits contractors with many small, scattered sites.

keyComponents.name: Front loader and bucket
keyComponents.role: Scoops, carries and loads material, and acts as a front anchor when digging.

keyComponents.name: Backhoe boom, dipper and bucket
keyComponents.role: The rear digging arm, used for trenches, pits and lifting.

keyComponents.name: Swing frame
keyComponents.role: Lets the backhoe arm pivot sideways across the rear of the machine.

keyComponents.name: Stabiliser legs
keyComponents.role: Hydraulic outriggers that lift and steady the machine while it digs.

keyComponents.name: Torque converter and shuttle transmission
keyComponents.role: Give smooth starts and quick forward-reverse changes for loader work.

keyComponents.name: Axles
keyComponents.role: Rear drive with optional four-wheel drive for traction on soft ground.

applications: Water, sewer and telecoms trenching in towns and estates
Municipal works: drain clearing, road patching and small excavations
Foundation digging for residential buildings
Loading tippers with sand and gravel on smaller sites
Farm drainage, feed handling and general estate maintenance
Pipe laying and backfilling on the same visit
choosingTips: Choose 4WD if you work on soft, wet or sandy ground, where it makes a large difference to traction.
Check backhoe dig depth against your deepest regular trench.
An extending dipper adds reach and depth for utility work. Ask about availability for the model you want.
Consider auxiliary hydraulics if you want to run a breaker on the backhoe.
If you have several small sites, a backhoe that can drive itself between them saves transport costs.

Check the air filter indicator

Check tyre pressure and wheel nuts
Inspect the bucket teeth on both buckets
Look for hydraulic hose damage, especially at the swing frame

Check belt tension and the battery

maintenance.note: These intervals reflect general industry practice and are a guide only. Always follow the LiuGong operation and maintenance manual for your model and serial number.

safety: Deploy the stabilisers and lower the front bucket before digging
Locate buried cables and pipes before trenching. Utility strikes are a major hazard in urban work
Keep people out of the backhoe's swing arc
Lock the backhoe in its transport position before travelling on roads, and follow traffic rules
Never use the backhoe to lift people

faq.q: Backhoe loader or mini excavator: which should I choose?
faq.a: A backhoe loader can load as well as dig and can drive between sites, which suits varied municipal and utility work. A mini excavator digs more efficiently, rotates a full 360° and fits tighter spaces, but it needs a trailer between sites.

faq.q: Why use the stabilisers?
faq.a: They take load off the tyres and form a firm base, so the machine does not bounce or slide while digging. That improves both safety and digging accuracy.

faq.q: Is 4WD necessary?
faq.a: On paved or dry, firm ground 2WD is often enough. On wet, sandy or uneven sites, which are common in the rainy season, 4WD gives much better traction for loading.

faq.q: Can a backhoe loader run a hydraulic breaker?
faq.a: Yes, if the backhoe has auxiliary hydraulic piping and the breaker is matched to the machine's flow and weight. It is a common setup for road repair and small demolition jobs.

families.name: Rollers & Compactors
families.summary: Vibratory rollers that compact soil, sub-base and asphalt to the density road and building specifications require.
families.howItWorks:
Compaction squeezes the air out of soil, aggregate or asphalt so the layer becomes dense, strong and resistant to water and settlement. A roller does this with a combination of **static weight** and **vibration**.

Inside each vibrating drum is an **eccentric weight** on a shaft spun by a hydraulic motor. As it spins, it makes the drum hammer the ground many times a second. Two numbers describe that action. **Frequency** (Hz) is how many impacts per second. **Amplitude** (mm) is how far the drum moves up and down. **Centrifugal force** (kN) is the impact force. Many rollers offer two settings: **high amplitude / low frequency** pushes energy deep into thick soil lifts, and **low amplitude / high frequency** compacts thinner layers without crushing aggregate or cracking asphalt.

**Single-drum soil rollers** have one heavy smooth or padfoot drum at the front and rubber-tyred drive wheels at the rear, joined by an articulation joint. They suit earthworks, subgrade and granular base. A **padfoot** drum kneads cohesive soils such as clay. **Tandem (double-drum) rollers** have two steel drums, usually both vibrating, and finish asphalt and thin base layers. They carry **water spray systems** that wet the drums so hot asphalt does not stick. **Pneumatic-tyred rollers** use a row of rubber tyres to knead and seal asphalt surfaces.

Most modern rollers use **hydrostatic drive**. A hydraulic pump feeds motors in the drum and the axle, giving smooth starts and stops, which matters because a jerky stop can leave marks in fresh asphalt.

keyComponents.name: Eccentric vibration system

keyComponents.name: Hydrostatic drive

keyComponents.name: Articulation joint
keyComponents.role: Steers the machine and keeps the drum tracking evenly over the surface.

keyComponents.role: Keeps the drums wet so asphalt does not stick.

keyComponents.name: Scrapers

faq.q: When should I use high or low amplitude?
faq.a: High amplitude drives energy deep into thick soil lifts. Low amplitude, at higher frequency, suits thinner layers and asphalt, where too much force can crush aggregate or crack the mat.

faq.q: Smooth drum or padfoot?
faq.a: Smooth drums suit granular soils, sand, gravel and laterite base. Padfoot drums knead cohesive soils such as clay, which a smooth drum tends to bridge over without compacting fully.

faq.q: Why do asphalt rollers spray water?
faq.a: Hot asphalt sticks to a dry steel drum and tears the surface. A thin film of water on the drum prevents this.

faq.q: How many passes does compaction need?
faq.a: It depends on the material, the lift thickness, the moisture and the specification. Contractors usually set the number with a trial section and check density with field tests.

families.name: Mining Trucks
families.summary: Wide-body mining trucks for hauling rock, ore and overburden in quarries and mines.
families.howItWorks:
An off-highway mining truck is a heavy hauler built for short, repeated trips between a loading face and a crusher, stockpile or waste dump. These routes are often steep and rough. Its frame, axles and suspension are far heavier than a road tipper's, and it is sized to be filled in a few passes by a large excavator or wheel loader.

The diesel engine drives through an **automatic or powershift transmission** with a torque converter, so the truck can climb loaded up ramps and start smoothly on grades. Power goes through a drive shaft to **rear drive axles**, which use heavy reduction gearing to turn high engine speed into strong wheel torque. A **6x4** layout, with three axles of which two are driven, spreads the load over more tyres.

The **body** is a thick steel box, usually with a sloped floor and no tailgate, so blasted rock slides out cleanly. Large **hoist cylinders** tip it. Spec sheets give two capacities: **struck** (level full) and **heaped** (with a natural mound on top). Along with **rated payload**, these tell you how many loader or excavator passes fill the truck.

Slowing a loaded truck on a downhill ramp is as important as climbing it. Mining trucks use heavy-duty service brakes and often an engine or exhaust brake or a retarder to control speed without overheating the brakes.

keyComponents.name: Hoist cylinders

keyComponents.role: Gives smooth, automatic or powershift gear changes for loaded climbs and descents.

keyComponents.name: Drive axles

Check haul road grades and lengths, which decide the power and retarding capacity you need.
Tyre costs dominate running costs, so invest in well-maintained haul roads.
Choose a rock-lined body for abrasive or heavy blasted material.

Drain the fuel water separator
Check tyre pressure, cuts and embedded rock

maintenance.note: These intervals reflect general industry practice and are a guide only. Always follow the LiuGong operation and maintenance manual for your model and serial number.

safety: Large trucks have big blind spots, so use site traffic rules, berms and radio communication
Never raise the body under power lines, and dump only on level, stable ground
Keep loaded descents within the retarding capacity of the truck
Never stand beside or behind a truck while it is dumping
Use the body prop or safety pin before working under a raised body

faq.q: What is the difference between struck and heaped capacity?
faq.a: Struck capacity is the body filled level to the top. Heaped capacity adds the natural mound that forms above the sides. Payload in kg is the limit that matters for dense rock.

faq.q: How do I match a truck to my excavator or loader?
faq.a: Divide the truck's payload by the weight of material the loading machine carries per bucket. Three to five passes is usually efficient. Too many passes leaves the truck waiting, and too few overloads the loading tool.

faq.q: Can a mining truck be driven on public roads?
faq.a: Generally not. Off-highway trucks are built wider and heavier than road limits allow and are meant for haul roads inside the site. They are moved between sites on low-bed trailers.

faq.q: What drives tyre wear on haul trucks?
faq.a: The main causes are under-inflation, overloading, sharp rock spillage, poorly drained haul roads and tight, fast turns. Graded, well-drained haul roads with spillage cleared regularly are the best way to extend tyre life.
